title: The names at the end
hook: He is Allah, the King, the Holy, Peace, the Faithful … the Creator, the Fashioner (59:22–24)

segments.voice: Yesterday, a mountain humbled, and your line was the mountain would crumble. Which line did you read slowly, and did it move anything? Today, the very end of Surah Al-Hashr. Day six hundred twenty-one.

Anyone who has written a birthday card for their mother knows the problem. One word won't do. Kind, but also stubborn. Funny, and also the one who stayed up when you were sick. Every word catches one side and misses the rest, so the card turns into a list. Surah Al-Hashr ends with a list too. Three verses, each beginning He is Allah, and then names, one after another, eleven of them in the last two verses alone.
screen: `HE IS ALLAH, HE IS ALLAH, HE IS ALLAH.`

segments.voice: Verse twenty-two: he is God, other than whom there is no god, the knower of the unseen and the seen, the Merciful, the Compassionate. Verse twenty-three, in Pickthall: "He is Allah, than Whom there is no other God, the Sovereign Lord, the Holy One, Peace, the Keeper of Faith, the Guardian, the Majestic, the Compeller, the Superb." In Arabic: al-Malik, al-Quddus, as-Salam, al-Mu'min, al-Muhaymin, al-'Aziz, al-Jabbar, al-Mutakabbir. Eight names in a single breath. Then verse twenty-four. Pickthall: "He is Allah, the Creator, the Shaper out of naught, the Fashioner. His are the most beautiful names." Al-Khaliq, al-Bari', al-Musawwir. Commentators tell these three apart like stages of making: al-Khaliq determines and plans, al-Bari' brings into being, al-Musawwir gives each thing its form. Planner, maker, shaper. Then the phrase that names the whole idea: lahul-asma'ul-husna, his are the most beautiful names. And the surah ends where it began: everything in the heavens and the earth glorifies him. A hadith in Bukhari and Muslim says God has ninety-nine names, and whoever learns and keeps them enters paradise. The familiar list of ninety-nine comes from a report in Tirmidhi, and many scholars think that list was gathered by narrators rather than spoken by the Prophet ﷺ himself. But the names in these three verses are straight from the Qur'an, and many Muslims know them by heart. No single name says it all. That's why there are so many.
screen: `THE KNOWER OF THE UNSEEN AND SEEN.` · `EIGHT NAMES IN ONE BREATH.` · `PLANNER, MAKER, SHAPER.` · `HIS ARE THE MOST BEAUTIFUL NAMES.`

segments.voice: The practice: recite these names. Sit, and let the breath slow. If you pray, recite the names of verse twenty-three slowly, one per breath: al-Malik, al-Quddus, as-Salam, al-Mu'min, and on, letting each settle before the next. If that isn't yours, take three of the English words, Peace, the Holy, the Fashioner, and let one sit on each out-breath. Notice which one stays with you. The bell holds the time.
The names at the end. Surah Al-Hashr closes with names of God, from the Sovereign to the Fashioner, and says his are the most beautiful names. Today's word.
screen: `THE NAMES AT THE END — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: his are the beautiful names. Today, notice one moment that fits one name: peace, making, guarding, and name it to yourself. Day six hundred twenty-one.

howItsDone: Many Muslims recite the last three verses of Surah Al-Hashr, especially morning and evening, and learn the names of God, often from the list of ninety-nine, as a form of remembrance.

fork.setup: you have three names: al-Khaliq, al-Bari', al-Musawwir. how do commentators tell them apart?
options: they're three ways of saying the same thing.
planner, maker, shaper: stages of making.
creator of heaven, earth and sea.
fork.reveal: many commentators read them as stages: determining, bringing into being, and giving form.

original.note: Arabic: his are the most beautiful names. al-asma' al-husna is the phrase Muslims use for the names of God.

trapdoor: what you thought: a list of God's titles.
what it means: names turned one by one, because no single name can say it all.

what a scholar hears: three verses each opening huwa Allah; khaliq, bari', musawwir as stages of creation; al-asma' al-husna also in 7:180, 17:110, 20:8; Bukhari 2736 / Muslim 2677 on ninety-nine names, the list itself in Tirmidhi 3507.
